cards.text: This is 1 Chronicles, and it opens with one big family tree, starting at the very top with Adam, the first man (1 Corinthians 15:45). No ages, no stories, just names, like the book walked in and started reading the guest list. The names run down to the man who went into the ark because of the flood (Genesis 7:7).

cards.question: The list runs from Adam down to the man who went into the ark. Who is he?
Then the family tree splits three ways. Noah's sons are Shem, Ham and ___.

cards.text: Next come the families that came from Noah's three sons. Two names stand out. Nimrod began to be a mighty one on the earth. And Peleg got his name because in his days the earth was divided. Imagine your whole lifetime getting summed up by one headline.

Then the list zooms in on one line from Shem: Arphaxad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, and on down through Terah. Friend, I practiced saying Arphaxad in the mirror ALL week, and every single time it comes out like a sneeze. Bless me.

cards.question: After all those names, the line from Shem finally lands on a name you KNOW. Who is it?
Abraham has two sons. Who are they?

cards.text: Abraham's son Ishmael has twelve sons, starting with his firstborn, Nebaioth, then Kedar, and Keturah, Abraham's concubine, has six more sons, Midian among them. Friend, I raised six cookie cutters and STILL called Chip "Sparkle" twice a week, so twelve? I'd just yell "HEY, SON" and see who turns around.

cards.question: Abraham's son Isaac has two sons. Who are they?

cards.text: Israel is the man also called Jacob (Genesis 32:28). The list follows the family of Esau, that is, Edom (Genesis 36:1), Amalek among them, and then the family of Seir the Horite (Genesis 36:20). That's a LOT of cousins, friend. You'd need a whole group chat just to plan the cookie exchange.

cards.question: The list turns to the kings who reigned in Edom. They reigned before any king reigned over whom?

cards.text: Eight kings reign in Edom. Over and over, a king dies and someone reigns in his place, until the last one, Hadad, dies. Then comes a list of Edom's chiefs, and that's the whole chapter. Adam to Edom in ONE sitting, friend? Back in the junk drawer, it took me three weeks to get past a rubber band.

findings.problem: The genealogies, name lists and repeated king-succession list are long stretches of detail, yet cards 2, 3, 6, 7, 9 and 11 all quiz them. These stretches should be summarized, not used for choice cards.

rule.text: A long stretch never gets a choice card.

findings.problem: Five non-opening story cards exceed the two-sentence limit: card 4 has five sentences, card 5 has three, card 8 has three, card 10 has four and card 12 has five.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Five of the six choice cards are multiple choice and the other is fill in the blank, so multiple choice dominates the stop by a wide margin.

rule.text: No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: Japheth has not appeared in the earlier cards, and nothing in the setup lets the baker infer the third son's name. The blank tests unseen wording or recall rather than a meaning the baker can reason out.

rule.text: The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The question states without qualification that Abraham has two sons. Verses 32-33 then list six sons born to Keturah, and card 8 calls them six more sons, so the question needs to identify Isaac and Ishmael as the two sons named in verse 28 rather than implying they were Abraham's only sons.

rule.text: He never says anything the text shows is wrong.
